en.title: Soil Science: the whole course
en.short: What soil science is, how soil degrees are organised, the main areas, how to study, and common mistakes.

sections.heading: What the subject is
sections.text:
Soil science is the study of soil as a natural body: the loose layer at the earth’s surface where rock, water, air, dead plant material and living organisms meet and react. It asks what soil is made of, how it formed, how it behaves physically, chemically and biologically, and how people can use it without destroying it.

Soil is a three-phase system: mineral particles and organic matter (solid), water carrying dissolved salts (liquid) and air (gas). Their proportions change with rainfall, drainage and management, and those changes decide whether crops grow well.

The subject is both a natural science and an applied one. Pedology studies soil formation and classification. Edaphology studies soil as a medium for plants. Soil science borrows from geology, chemistry, physics, biology and geography, and it feeds into agriculture, engineering, environmental management and land planning.

sections.heading: How a degree is usually organised
sections.text:
Length and awards differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook. In Nigeria a BSc is commonly four years, and programmes follow benchmark documents from the National Universities Commission. Polytechnics, under the National Board for Technical Education, award the ND and HND in agriculture and related fields, and colleges of education award the NCE. In the United Kingdom a BSc is usually three years (four in Scotland); in the United States a bachelor’s degree is usually four. A master’s is typically one to two years and often ends with a dissertation or thesis.

The early years build science foundations: chemistry, biology, physics, mathematics and geology, with introductory soil science and field work. Later years add soil chemistry, fertility, conservation, survey and management, and usually a final-year project. A master’s goes deeper into theory and methods.

sections.heading: The main areas in teaching order
sections.text:
Introductory topics come first: the scope and history of the subject, soil in the ecosystem, soil-forming factors and processes, the soil profile and classification, minerals and parent material, organic matter and humus, texture, structure and bulk density, soil water, and soil air and heat.

The core then turns to chemistry and biology: pH, cation exchange and buffering, colloids and nutrient sorption, soil organisms, and the carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, sulphur and micronutrient cycles. From there the course moves to use and management: soil fertility and plant nutrition, fertilisers and manures, erosion and conservation, land evaluation, soil survey and remote sensing, moisture measurement and water balance, irrigation and drainage, saline, sodic and acid soils, pollution and remediation, and the soils of Nigeria and Africa.

Later core topics connect soil to wider questions: land use change and soil carbon, soil biology in sustainable agriculture, soil health indicators, professional practice and ethics, and research methods for the final project. Master’s level covers advanced pedology and geomorphology, advanced chemistry and mineralogy, spatial modelling and pedometrics, and dissertation methods.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Soil science is learned by looking, touching and measuring. Handle samples, feel texture between your fingers, and read a profile in a pit or a road cut. A description you have written yourself is remembered far better than one you have read.

Learn each topic at three levels: the definition, the mechanism, and the management consequence. For example, know what cation exchange capacity is, why clay type and organic matter control it, and what it means for liming and fertiliser choice.

Do the calculations by hand, keep units consistent, and record the date and place of every field measurement. Practise describing a profile in the standard order used in your department.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text:
Students mix up soil texture (the proportions of sand, silt and clay) with structure (how particles are grouped). They confuse ions in the soil solution with exchangeable ions held on colloids. They report pH without saying whether it was measured in water or in a salt solution, though the two values differ.

In the field, many students describe colour or depth loosely and forget to record slope, drainage and land use. In the laboratory, they skip replicates and do not check a reading against a known standard.

In assignments, the commonest error is to treat one country’s classification or fertiliser recommendation as universal. Name the system and the country, and check the current official source before quoting any figure.

keyPoints: Soil is a three-phase system of solids, water and air, and its behaviour follows from their proportions.
Pedology studies how soils form and are classified; edaphology studies soil as a medium for plants.
Degree length and awards differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook.
Learn every topic at three levels: definition, mechanism and management consequence.
Texture is the proportion of sand, silt and clay; structure is how the particles are grouped.
Always state the method, the country and the date behind a soil figure or classification.

en.title: Soil Science: Scope, Branches and History
en.short: What soil is, the main branches of soil science, and how Dokuchaev founded pedology.

sections.heading: What soil is
sections.text: Soil is a natural body at the Earth’s surface. It is made of mineral particles from weathered rock, organic matter from dead plants and animals, water, air and living organisms. These parts interact. Soil is not just dirt or powdered rock: it has structure, pore spaces and layers. It supports plant roots, stores water and nutrients, and filters water. Its properties vary from place to place and change over time.

sections.heading: Main branches
sections.text: Soil science is the study of soil as a natural body and as a resource. It has two broad divisions. Pedology studies soil formation, classification and distribution. Edaphology studies soil in relation to plants, including fertility. The main branches are soil physics (texture, structure, water, air and heat), soil chemistry (minerals, pH, ion exchange and chemical reactions), soil biology (soil organisms and their processes) and soil fertility (nutrient supply and plant nutrition). Applied branches include soil survey, conservation, land evaluation, irrigation and pollution. The branches overlap; soil fertility, for example, draws on physics, chemistry and biology.

sections.heading: Dokuchaev and pedology
sections.text: In the late nineteenth century, Vasily Dokuchaev, a Russian geologist and soil scientist, studied the black chernozem soils of the steppes. He argued that soil is an independent natural body formed by the interaction of climate, organisms, relief (slope and landscape shape), parent material (the material the soil forms from) and time. This was a change from treating soil as loose rock debris. His five factors became the foundation of pedology. Hans Jenny later presented them as factors of soil formation, and many courses now add human activity. A simple case: two fields on the same parent material but with different slope and vegetation can develop different soils, because water and organic inputs differ. Soil is therefore a product of its environment, not just broken rock.

keyPoints: Soil is a natural body of mineral particles, organic matter, water, air and living organisms.
Soil science has two broad divisions: pedology and edaphology.
Pedology studies soil formation, classification and distribution; edaphology studies soil in relation to plants.
Main branches include soil physics, soil chemistry, soil biology and soil fertility.
Vasily Dokuchaev argued that soil is an independent natural body formed by climate, organisms, relief, parent material and time.
These five factors became the foundation of pedology, and human activity is often added today.

en.title: Soil in the Ecosystem and the Critical Zone
en.short: Soil functions in the critical zone, links between Earth spheres, and how degradation spreads.

sections.heading: The critical zone
sections.text: The critical zone is the thin outer layer of the Earth where rock, soil, water, air and living things meet. It reaches from the tops of plants down to the bottom of groundwater. Soil is its central part: a porous mixture of minerals, organic matter, water, air and organisms. Because soil sits at this meeting point, changes in soil affect the whole zone.

sections.heading: Functions for life
sections.text: Soil has several functions that support life. It is a medium for plant growth, holding roots and supplying water and nutrients. It stores water after rain and filters it as it moves down. It cycles carbon, nitrogen and other elements as organisms decompose matter. It also gives engineering support: foundations, roads and embankments rely on soil strength and stability. These functions work together, not separately.

sections.heading: Links between spheres
sections.text: Soil links the atmosphere, biosphere, hydrosphere and lithosphere. Gases enter and leave soil air, so soil affects the atmosphere. Roots and soil organisms are part of the biosphere, and dead matter returns to soil. Water moves through soil to groundwater and streams, linking the hydrosphere. Weathered rock from the lithosphere supplies soil minerals. A change in one link can pass to the others.

sections.heading: Degradation harms all
sections.text: Degradation of one function harms the others. On Amina’s maize field near Kano, heavy trampling by cattle compacts the soil. Rain then infiltrates less, so more runs off. Roots grow poorly, plants take up less water and nutrients, and topsoil erodes. The runoff carries soil into a nearby stream, and carbon and nitrogen are lost from the field. The same runoff also weakens support for a store building, washing soil from its foundations. One problem has damaged plant growth, water storage, nutrient cycling and engineering support.

keyPoints: The critical zone is the outer layer where rock, soil, water, air and life interact.
Soil supports plant growth, stores and filters water, cycles elements and gives engineering support.
Soil links the atmosphere, biosphere, hydrosphere and lithosphere.
Damage to one soil function usually harms the others.
Compaction reduces infiltration and root growth, and increases runoff and erosion.
The Kano case shows how one soil problem can damage several functions at once.

en.title: Soil-Forming Factors and Processes
en.short: The five soil-forming factors, the four soil processes, and residual versus transported soils.

sections.heading: Five state factors
sections.text: Soil formation is controlled by five state factors: climate, organisms, relief, parent material and time. Climate supplies water and heat. Organisms include plants, animals, microbes and people. Relief means slope and position in the landscape. Parent material is the mineral or organic material the soil develops from. Time is the period of development. These factors are controls, not processes. A common shorthand is S = f(cl, o, r, p, t), meaning soil S is a function of the five factors. Changing one factor can change the soil, but the factors also interact.

sections.heading: Four soil processes
sections.text: Within those controls, four groups of processes build a profile. Additions bring material in: leaf litter, roots, animal wastes, dust, and material deposited by water or wind. Losses remove material: erosion, leaching of soluble salts, gas loss, and nutrient uptake by plants. Transformations change material in place: weathering of minerals, decomposition of organic matter, mineralisation, and humus formation. Translocation moves material within the soil. Downward movement is eluviation; deposition lower down is illuviation. Clay, iron oxides and humus can move this way. These processes act together, so a profile is a record of gains, losses, changes and movement.

sections.heading: Residual and transported soils
sections.text: A residual soil forms from rock or material that lies beneath it and stays in place. A transported soil forms from material carried in and deposited. Alluvial soil is deposited by rivers and streams. Colluvial soil is moved downslope by gravity. Aeolian soil is deposited by wind. Lacustrine soil is deposited in lakes. For example, on a hillslope near Abeokuta, Nigeria, a thin residual soil may sit on bedrock, while colluvium collects at the footslope. A river terrace nearby may carry alluvium. The name describes the deposit, not the current climate.

keyPoints: The five state factors are climate, organisms, relief, parent material and time.
State factors control soil formation; additions, losses, transformations and translocation are the processes.
Additions and losses change what is in the soil; transformations change it in place; translocation moves it within the profile.
Eluviation is removal and illuviation is deposition within the soil.
Residual soils form in place from underlying material; transported soils form from material brought by water, gravity or wind.
Alluvial, colluvial, aeolian and lacustrine soils are named for their transport and deposition environment.

en.title: Soil Profile, Horizons and Classification
en.short: Reading a soil profile: O, A, E, B, C and R horizons, and the USDA and WRB classification systems.

sections.heading: The soil profile
sections.text: A soil profile is a vertical section through soil, from the surface down to parent material or bedrock. It is divided into horizons, layers that differ in colour, texture, structure, organic matter and chemistry. The main layers are called master horizons.

sections.heading: Master horizons
sections.text: O is an organic horizon, dominated by plant litter or peat. A is a mineral topsoil with accumulated humus and roots. E is an eluvial horizon, pale because clay, iron or aluminium have been washed downward. B is a subsoil horizon of accumulation, strong structure or altered colour. C is weathered parent material with little soil development. R is hard, continuous bedrock. Subscripts add detail: Bt means clay accumulation. A humid forest profile may read O-A-E-Bt-C; a shallow profile on granite may read A-C-R.

sections.heading: Separating horizons
sections.text: Properties used to separate horizons include colour, texture, structure, organic matter, roots, carbonate, mottling and gleying. A dark A under grass may be 20 cm thick; below it a pale E, then a clay-rich Bt, then a C. Depth and boundary shape also matter. A horizon is not a fixed depth: it is defined by its properties.

sections.heading: Classification systems
sections.text: USDA Soil Taxonomy is a hierarchical system used mainly in the United States and widely elsewhere. It uses diagnostic horizons, which are horizons used as classification criteria, and soil moisture and temperature regimes. WRB, the World Reference Base for Soil Resources, is an international system supported by FAO (Food and Agriculture Organization) and the International Union of Soil Sciences. It uses diagnostic horizons, properties and materials, then qualifiers, which are extra descriptive terms. A common system is needed because soil maps, research and land-use advice must be comparable across borders; otherwise the same soil may carry different local names. Classification keys are revised, so check the current official version.

keyPoints: A soil profile is a vertical section from the surface to parent material or bedrock.
O is organic; A is mineral topsoil with humus; E is leached and pale; B is subsoil of accumulation or alteration; C is weathered parent material; R is bedrock.
Horizons are separated by properties such as colour, texture, structure, organic matter, roots and carbonate.
Horizon depth is not fixed; it is defined by properties and boundaries.
USDA Soil Taxonomy is hierarchical and uses diagnostic horizons and moisture and temperature regimes.
WRB is an international system using diagnostic horizons, properties and materials plus qualifiers; common names make maps and research comparable.

en.title: Soil Minerals and Parent Material
en.short: Primary and secondary minerals, weathering, and how they set texture, surface area and water and nutrient retention.

sections.heading: Primary minerals
sections.text: Primary minerals form in igneous or metamorphic rock and survive into soil as grains. Quartz (silicon dioxide) is hard and resists weathering, so it remains as sand and silt. Feldspars are aluminosilicates with potassium, sodium or calcium; they weather more readily than quartz. Mica, hornblende and olivine are also primary but less stable. These minerals give young or sandy soils much of their skeleton. Their surfaces are small compared with clay, so they hold little water or nutrients.

sections.heading: Secondary clay minerals
sections.text: Secondary minerals form by weathering or precipitation. Clay minerals are layered aluminosilicates, less than 2 micrometres across. Surface area is the exposed area per gram. Kaolinite has a 1:1 layer structure and low surface area and little electrical charge. Illite is 2:1 but non-expanding, with potassium between layers. Montmorillonite is 2:1 and expanding; water enters between layers, giving very high surface area. In general montmorillonite holds more water and nutrients than illite, and illite more than kaolinite. These differences affect swelling, workability and droughtiness.

sections.heading: Weathering and parent material
sections.text: Parent material sets the starting minerals. Granite is rich in quartz and feldspar; basalt is richer in iron and magnesium minerals that weather quickly. Climate and drainage set the weathering stage. Young soils keep primary minerals. Moderate weathering in base-rich conditions favours illite and montmorillonite. Strong leaching in hot, wet climates leaves quartz and kaolinite. Thus a humid tropical soil may be clay-rich but low in nutrient-holding capacity because kaolinite dominates.

sections.heading: A small case
sections.text: On a granite hill in Jos, Nigeria, a farmer may find sandy, quartz-rich soil. After long weathering, the clay present is often kaolinite. It drains quickly and holds few nutrients, so manure and mulching help. In a drier, base-rich area, montmorillonite clay can make soil sticky when wet and cracked when dry, but it stores more water and nutrients. The lesson is that clay content alone is not enough: mineral type matters.

keyPoints: Primary minerals form in rock and remain in soil; quartz resists weathering while feldspars weather more easily.
Secondary clay minerals form by weathering and are clay-sized layered aluminosilicates.
Kaolinite is 1:1 and low in surface area; illite is non-expanding 2:1; montmorillonite is expanding 2:1 with high surface area.
Greater surface area and electrical charge generally increase water and nutrient retention, in the order montmorillonite > illite > kaolinite.
Parent material sets the starting mineral suite, while climate and drainage set the weathering stage.
Strong weathering in hot, wet climates often leaves quartz and kaolinite, so a clay-rich soil may still hold few nutrients.

en.title: Soil Organic Matter and Humus
en.short: Fresh residues, living biomass and stable humus, their breakdown, and how organic matter improves soil.

sections.heading: Three pools
sections.text: Soil organic matter (SOM) is all organic material in soil. Separate three pools. Fresh residues are recently added litter, roots and manure; they feed decomposers. Living biomass is the roots, bacteria, fungi and animals alive at one time. It is small but active. Humus is the dark, stable material left after much decomposition. It is not one substance but a mixture of large organic molecules and microbial products, often protected by clay and aggregates. Humus breaks down slowly and stores carbon and nutrients.

sections.heading: Decomposition and humification
sections.text: Decomposition is the breakdown of residues by soil organisms. They use carbon for energy and release carbon dioxide, water and mineral nutrients. Some carbon and nitrogen become microbial cells. Humification is the transformation of remaining residues and microbial products into complex, dark organic matter. So fresh residues feed the living biomass, and both leave humus. The balance depends on inputs, temperature, moisture, aeration, clay and the carbon-to-nitrogen ratio. A farmer in Kaduna who returns maize stover and adds manure keeps the cycle supplied; burning residues and removing all stover depletes it.

sections.heading: Benefits and management
sections.text: Organic matter raises cation exchange capacity (CEC), the ability to hold exchangeable cations such as calcium, magnesium, potassium and ammonium. Its negative charges reduce leaching. It also raises water holding capacity and aggregate stability. Organic glues and fungal threads bind particles into crumbs that resist erosion and let water and air enter. These benefits are largest in sandy soils. To build organic matter, add manure, compost, residues or mulch, grow cover crops, rotate crops, reduce tillage and keep soil covered. Burning residues, removing all stover, overgrazing and erosion deplete it. Build-up is slow; check local extension advice for rates.

keyPoints: SOM has three useful pools: fresh residues, living biomass and stable humus.
Decomposition releases carbon dioxide and nutrients; humification forms stable dark organic matter.
Organic matter raises CEC by holding exchangeable cations and reducing leaching.
Organic matter improves water holding and aggregate stability, especially in sandy soils.
Adding residues, manure, compost and cover crops builds organic matter; burning, removal and erosion deplete it.
Build-up is slow and depends on climate, texture and residue quality; follow local advice.

en.title: Soil Physics: Texture, Structure and Bulk Density
en.short: Soil separates, textural classes and triangles, structure, bulk density, porosity and effects on roots, air and water.

sections.heading: Texture and separates
sections.text: Soil texture is the relative amounts of sand, silt and clay, called soil separates. In the USDA (United States) system, sand is 2.0 to 0.05 mm, silt is 0.05 to 0.002 mm, and clay is less than 0.002 mm. Other systems differ; check your course. The separates are grouped into textural classes such as sandy, loamy and clayey. Texture is an important property because it affects pore size, water retention and nutrient behaviour.

sections.heading: Triangle and structure
sections.text: A textural triangle plots the three percentages, which must sum to 100. Read the clay value on its axis, then the sand value, following the grid lines; the point where they meet gives the class. Structure is how soil particles are bound into peds, aggregates. Common types are granular, blocky, prismatic or columnar, platy, and massive or single grain. Structure creates pores: granular and blocky soils have many large pores (macropores), while platy or massive soils may restrict vertical flow.

sections.heading: Bulk density and porosity
sections.text: Bulk density is the oven-dry mass of soil divided by its bulk volume, including pores. Particle density is the mass of the solid particles divided by their own volume; for many mineral soils it is about 2.65 g/cm³. Porosity is the pore fraction: porosity = 1 − (bulk density ÷ particle density). A compacted soil has high bulk density and low porosity. High bulk density increases root resistance and reduces macropores, so roots, air and water move less freely.

sections.heading: Worked example and effects
sections.text: Take 100 cm³ of soil with oven-dry mass 130 g. Bulk density = 130 ÷ 100 = 1.30 g/cm³. With particle density 2.65 g/cm³, porosity = 1 − (1.30 ÷ 2.65) = 1 − 0.491 = 0.509, about 51%. The pore volume is 0.509 × 100 = 50.9 cm³. Texture and structure decide pore sizes. Coarse sandy soil drains quickly and holds little water; fine clayey soil holds more water but may be poorly aerated. Good structure and moderate bulk density give roots room, air and water.

keyPoints: Soil texture is the relative amounts of sand, silt and clay separates.
On a textural triangle, the three percentages sum to 100 and their intersection gives the class.
Structure is the arrangement of particles into peds; common types are granular, blocky, prismatic or columnar, platy and massive.
Bulk density = oven-dry mass ÷ bulk volume; porosity = 1 − (bulk density ÷ particle density).
High bulk density and low porosity restrict roots, aeration and water movement.
Texture and structure control pore sizes, so they affect water retention, drainage and air supply.

en.title: Soil Water: Retention, Movement and Availability
en.short: Soil water classes, field capacity, wilting point, available water and Darcy flow.

sections.heading: Kinds of soil water
sections.text: Soil water is held in pores and on particle surfaces. Gravitational water fills large pores and drains downward under gravity after rain or irrigation; it may be lost below the root zone. Capillary water is held in small pores by surface tension and adhesion. It is the main supply for roots. Hygroscopic water is a thin film tightly adsorbed to soil particles, especially clay and organic matter. It is held very strongly and is effectively unavailable to plants. These categories are not fixed: water moves between them as the soil wets and dries.

sections.heading: Field capacity and AWC
sections.text: Field capacity is the water content after rapid drainage has largely stopped. It is often taken at a matric potential of about −10 to −33 kPa, depending on the soil and convention. Permanent wilting point is the water content at which plants can no longer extract water, commonly taken at −1,500 kPa (−1.5 MPa). Available water capacity (AWC) is the water held between these limits: AWC = FC − PWP, where FC and PWP are volumetric water contents. It is the reservoir roots can use.

sections.heading: Potential and Darcy’s law
sections.text: Water moves from higher total potential to lower. In unsaturated soil, matric potential is negative because adhesion and capillarity pull water into small pores; it becomes more negative as the soil dries. Darcy’s law is q = −K × (ΔH ÷ ΔL). Here q is flux (volume per area per time), K is hydraulic conductivity (how easily water flows through the soil pores), H is total head and L is distance. In saturated flow all pores are water-filled and K is constant. In unsaturated flow K falls sharply as water content and matric potential decrease.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Suppose FC = 0.30 and PWP = 0.12 m3/m3. AWC = 0.30 − 0.12 = 0.18 m3/m3. For a root zone 0.60 m deep, available water = 0.18 × 0.60 = 0.108 m = 108 mm. Each square metre holds 108 litres of available water. Check: 0.108 m3 per m2 = 108 L per m2.

keyPoints: Gravitational water drains under gravity, capillary water is held in small pores, and hygroscopic water is tightly adsorbed and unavailable.
Field capacity is the water content after rapid drainage; permanent wilting point is the water content at which plants can no longer extract water.
Available water capacity is AWC = FC − PWP, with FC and PWP as volumetric water contents.
Water moves from higher to lower total potential, and matric potential is negative in unsaturated soil.
Darcy’s law is q = −K × (ΔH ÷ ΔL); saturated K is constant, while unsaturated K falls as the soil dries.
For a 0.60 m root zone with AWC 0.18 m3/m3, available water is 0.18 × 0.60 = 0.108 m = 108 mm.

en.title: Soil Air, Heat and Gas Exchange
en.short: How pore space shares air and water, soil heat flow and temperature, and gas diffusion.

sections.heading: Pore space and aeration
sections.text: Soil pores hold water and air. Total porosity is the pore fraction of bulk volume; air-filled porosity is the air fraction. If no air is trapped, air-filled porosity = total porosity − volumetric water content, where volumetric water content is water volume per bulk volume. As water rises, air falls. Roots and aerobic microbes use oxygen and release carbon dioxide. Oxygen diffuses much more slowly in water than in air, so wet, compact or fine-textured soil can be poorly aerated. About 10 per cent air-filled porosity is a rough lower limit for good root growth, but thresholds vary. Poor aeration reduces root growth, water uptake and aerobic decomposition, and favours denitrification and methane production.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Example: total porosity 0.50, volumetric water content 0.35. Air-filled porosity = 0.50 − 0.35 = 0.15, or 15 per cent. After irrigation water content is 0.45, so air-filled porosity = 0.50 − 0.45 = 0.05, or 5 per cent. Air space is now small and poorly connected, so oxygen supply is likely to limit roots and microbes.

sections.heading: Temperature and heat flow
sections.text: Soil temperature is driven by solar radiation and air temperature, modified by water, colour, mulch and vegetation. Heat moves mainly by conduction. Water conducts heat better than air, so wet soil warms and cools more slowly than dry soil. Daily and seasonal temperature waves are damped and delayed with depth. USDA Soil Taxonomy defines temperature regimes (frigid, mesic, thermic) from mean annual soil temperature and seasonal difference at 50 cm depth; check boundaries.

sections.heading: Gas diffusion
sections.text: Gas exchange with the atmosphere is mainly by diffusion along concentration gradients. Fick’s law gives flux = −D × (change in concentration ÷ distance), where D is the diffusion coefficient. In soil, D falls with low air-filled porosity, tortuous pores and water films. Oxygen moves in and carbon dioxide moves out; other gases follow their own gradients. Mass flow is usually small. Good aeration needs connected air-filled pores, not just large total porosity.

keyPoints: Air-filled porosity = total porosity − volumetric water content when no air is trapped.
Aeration limits roots and aerobic microbes because oxygen diffuses much more slowly in water than in air.
About 10 per cent air-filled porosity is a common rough guideline for good root growth, but thresholds vary.
Soil heat moves mainly by conduction, and water content strongly affects thermal conductivity and temperature swings.
Soil temperature regimes such as frigid, mesic and thermic are defined in USDA Soil Taxonomy and should be checked locally.
Gas exchange is mainly by diffusion: flux = −D × (change in concentration ÷ distance).

en.title: Soil Chemistry: pH, Cation Exchange and Buffering
en.short: Soil pH, acidity sources, exchange capacity, base saturation, lyotropic series, buffering and liming.

sections.heading: pH and acidity
sections.text:
Soil pH measures hydrogen ion activity: pH = −log10[H+]. The scale runs from 0 to 14; below 7 is acidic, 7 neutral, above 7 alkaline. State whether pH was measured in water or in dilute CaCl2.

Acidity comes mainly from H+ and exchangeable Al3+ on clay and humus, organic acids, and leaching of bases. Ammonium fertilisers, nitrification and root uptake add H+. Al3+ is the main toxic ion in strongly acid soils. Alkalinity comes from carbonates and exchangeable sodium.

sections.heading: Exchange capacity
sections.text: Cation exchange capacity (CEC) is the total negative charge that holds exchangeable cations, expressed in cmolc/kg or meq/100 g. It rises with clay and organic matter. Anion exchange capacity (AEC) is the positive charge that holds anions such as phosphate and sulphate; it matters in variable-charge oxides at low pH. Exchange retains nutrients against leaching but lets one cation displace another.

sections.heading: Base saturation and series
sections.text:
Base saturation is the percentage of CEC occupied by exchangeable bases (Ca2+, Mg2+, K+, Na+): (sum of bases ÷ CEC) × 100. The lyotropic series ranks ions by how strongly they are held: higher charge and smaller hydrated radius bind more strongly. For major cations the approximate order is Al3+ > Ca2+ > Mg2+ > K+ ≈ NH4+ > Na+.

Example: CEC = 12 cmolc/kg; bases = 6.0 Ca + 2.0 Mg + 0.5 K + 0.3 Na = 8.8 cmolc/kg. Base saturation = 8.8 ÷ 12 × 100 = 73.3%. Exchangeable acidity = 12 − 8.8 = 3.2 cmolc/kg. To reach 80% base saturation, add 0.80 × 12 − 8.8 = 0.8 cmolc/kg.

sections.heading: Buffering and liming
sections.text: Buffering is the resistance of soil pH to change. High CEC, clay, organic matter and free carbonate buffer strongly; sandy low-CEC soils change quickly. Liming decisions use target pH, exchangeable acidity, base saturation and a lime requirement test. Lime neutralises H+ and Al3+, raises base saturation and reduces Al toxicity. Overliming can lower micronutrient availability. Check local recommendations because target pH and lime quality vary.

keyPoints: Soil pH is the negative log of hydrogen ion activity: pH = −log10[H+]; below 7 is acidic and above 7 alkaline.
Soil acidity comes mainly from H+ and exchangeable Al3+ and from leaching of bases; alkalinity comes from carbonates and exchangeable sodium.
CEC is the negative charge holding exchangeable cations, while AEC is positive charge holding anions such as phosphate and sulphate.
Base saturation = (sum of exchangeable bases ÷ CEC) × 100.
The lyotropic series ranks ions by adsorption strength, approximately Al3+ > Ca2+ > Mg2+ > K+ ≈ NH4+ > Na+.
Buffering resists pH change; liming decisions use target pH, exchangeable acidity, base saturation and a lime requirement test.

en.title: Soil Colloids, Adsorption and Nutrient Reactions
en.short: Clay and humus surfaces, specific adsorption, and phosphorus fixation and release.

sections.heading: Colloidal surfaces
sections.text: Soil colloids are the smallest reactive particles, roughly below 2 micrometres. They include clay minerals, iron and aluminium oxides, and humus. Their large surface area per unit mass makes them the main sites of nutrient retention. Clay minerals are layered aluminosilicates. Kaolinite has a 1:1 layer structure and low charge; smectite has 2:1 layers and expands; oxides have variable charge. Humus is decomposed organic matter with many carboxyl and phenolic groups. These surfaces carry charge, so ions and molecules stick to them.

sections.heading: Charge and specific adsorption
sections.text: Negative charge on clay comes partly from isomorphous substitution, where a lower-charge cation replaces a higher-charge one in the crystal. This is permanent charge. Edge hydroxyl groups and humus groups give variable charge that changes with pH: more negative at high pH, more positive at low pH. Cation exchange is electrostatic and outer-sphere. Specific adsorption is stronger: an ion forms an inner-sphere complex by ligand exchange, sharing an oxygen with the surface. Phosphate is adsorbed this way on iron and aluminium oxides and clay edges.

sections.heading: Phosphorus fixation
sections.text: In soil solution, phosphorus occurs mainly as dihydrogen phosphate (H2PO4−) and hydrogen phosphate (HPO4²−), depending on pH. Phosphate can precipitate with iron and aluminium in acid soils, and with calcium in neutral to alkaline soils. These solids can later dissolve and release phosphate. Specific adsorption, precipitation and slow diffusion into micropores together cause fixation: the nutrient is held so tightly or far from roots that plants cannot take it up quickly. Fixed phosphorus is not lost from the soil, but it is less available. On a red clay soil rich in iron oxides, a farmer broadcasts soluble phosphate. Much is adsorbed or precipitated near the granules, so only a small share enters the soil solution in the first season. Band placement, organic matter and mycorrhizal fungi can reduce fixation losses.

keyPoints: Soil colloids are clay minerals, oxides and humus; their large surface area retains nutrients.
Permanent negative charge comes from isomorphous substitution; variable charge from edge and humus groups changes with pH.
Specific adsorption forms inner-sphere complexes by ligand exchange and is stronger than simple cation exchange.
Phosphate is adsorbed on iron and aluminium oxides and can precipitate with iron, aluminium or calcium.
Fixation holds phosphorus tightly or away from roots, so it is less available but not necessarily lost.
Band placement, organic matter and mycorrhizae can reduce fixation losses.

en.title: Soil Organisms and Biological Activity
en.short: The soil food web, decomposers and soil engineers, and how land use and tillage alter biological activity.

sections.heading: The soil food web
sections.text:
Soil organisms form a food web: energy flows from dead plant material and roots to microbes, then to grazers and predators. Bacteria are single-celled decomposers using simple sugars and root exudates. Fungi grow as hyphae, thread-like filaments, and break down tougher lignin and cellulose.

Protozoa and nematodes are tiny grazers; nematodes include bacterial feeders, fungal feeders, plant parasites and predators. Earthworms and termites are macrofauna, animals large enough to move soil. Each group is a link.

sections.heading: Decomposition and structure
sections.text:
Bacteria and fungi are the main decomposers. They release enzymes, break litter into smaller compounds, and respire carbon dioxide. Fungi also bind soil particles into aggregates with hyphae, improving structure.

Protozoa and nematodes eat microbes and excrete ammonium, making nitrogen available to plants. Earthworms fragment litter, pull it into burrows, mix soil and leave casts; their channels raise porosity and water infiltration. Termites, especially in tropical soils, digest wood with gut microbes, build galleries and mounds, and move clay and nutrients. Their effects can help or harm crops.

sections.heading: Land use and tillage
sections.text:
Land use changes the community. Clearing forest or grassland for crops lowers organic matter and microbial biomass, and reduces fungal dominance and large invertebrates.

Tillage is a disturbance: ploughing breaks hyphae and aggregates, exposes protected organic matter to oxygen, and speeds carbon loss. It favours bacteria over fungi and reduces earthworm numbers. No-till or reduced tillage with residues tends to protect aggregates and fungal networks. These shifts change nutrient cycling: faster decomposition means faster mineralisation, releasing plant-available nutrients, but also greater leaching and carbon loss.

sections.heading: Case in Nigeria
sections.text:
Consider Ade’s maize field in Oyo State, Nigeria. Under repeated ploughing and residue removal, the surface is bare and aggregates break down.

Bacterial activity may rise briefly, but organic matter and earthworm channels decline, so infiltration falls and erosion risk rises. With residue retention and reduced tillage, hyphae and burrows are less disturbed. Nutrient release becomes slower but steadier. Results depend on soil, climate and management.

keyPoints: The soil food web links decomposers, grazers, predators and ecosystem engineers.
Bacteria and fungi mineralise organic matter; fungi also bind aggregates.
Protozoa and nematodes graze microbes and release ammonium.
Earthworms and termites mix soil, create pores and casts, and redistribute nutrients.
Tillage breaks hyphae and aggregates, shifts communities toward bacteria and speeds carbon loss.
Reduced tillage and residue retention protect biological structure and slow nutrient release.

en.title: Carbon and Nitrogen Cycles in Soil
en.short: How carbon and nitrogen move through soil, and what that means for fertiliser timing and greenhouse gases.

sections.heading: Carbon cycle
sections.text: Soil carbon enters as plant and animal residues and microbial biomass. Soil organisms respire organic carbon to CO2; this is carbon mineralisation. Some carbon is built into microbial cells, and some becomes humus. Immobilisation is the microbial uptake of mineral nutrients, such as ammonium or nitrate, into organic forms. A residue with wide C:N ratio slows net release because microbes need nitrogen for growth.

sections.heading: Nitrogen transformations
sections.text: Organic nitrogen is mineralised to ammonium (ammonification). Nitrification is the oxidation of ammonium to nitrite and then nitrate by soil microbes. Nitrate is mobile and easily lost. Denitrification is the reduction of nitrate to N2 and N2O by bacteria in low-oxygen soil. Biological nitrogen fixation (BNF) converts atmospheric N2 to ammonia, mainly by symbiotic bacteria in legume roots and by free-living organisms. Immobilisation competes with plants for ammonium and nitrate.

sections.heading: C:N example and timing
sections.text: Suppose 1,000 kg residue contains 450 kg C and 5 kg N, so C:N = 450 ÷ 5 = 90. Using a rough target of C:N 25 for net mineralisation, total N needed = 450 ÷ 25 = 18 kg. The residue supplies 5 kg, so about 13 kg N may be immobilised before net release. This is an illustration; the target varies. Apply nitrogen fertiliser near crop demand, split dressings, and avoid application before heavy rain or waterlogging.

sections.heading: Greenhouse gases
sections.text: Nitrous oxide (N2O) is produced by nitrification and denitrification; it is a potent greenhouse gas. Excess fertiliser N, wet or compacted soil, and high nitrate increase losses. Denitrification also returns N2 to the atmosphere. Carbon losses appear as CO2 when organic matter is oxidised. Management aims to match N supply to demand, improve drainage and aeration, and build soil organic matter without over-fertilising.

keyPoints: Mineralisation releases CO2 from organic carbon and ammonium from organic nitrogen; immobilisation takes mineral nutrients into microbial biomass.
Nitrification converts ammonium to nitrate; denitrification converts nitrate to N2 and N2O in low-oxygen soil.
Biological nitrogen fixation converts atmospheric N2 to ammonia, especially in legume symbioses.
C:N ratio = kg C ÷ kg N; a wide ratio favours immobilisation and a narrow ratio favours net mineralisation.
Apply nitrogen when the crop can use it, split applications, and avoid waterlogged or soon-to-be-rainy conditions.
N2O from nitrification and denitrification is a potent greenhouse gas; excess N and poor aeration increase losses.

en.title: Nutrient Cycles: Phosphorus, Sulphur and Micronutrients
en.short: Phosphorus and sulphur chemistry, micronutrient availability, pH effects and crop symptoms.

sections.heading: Phosphorus chemistry
sections.text: Phosphorus comes from apatite minerals, organic matter and fertiliser. Plants absorb mainly H2PO4− and HPO4²−, in proportions set by pH. Phosphorus is strongly fixed: it is adsorbed on clay and iron or aluminium oxides, or precipitated as calcium, iron or aluminium phosphates. Fixation reduces the labile pool, the fraction that can enter solution quickly. Available P is greatest in slightly acid to near neutral soil. At low pH, iron and aluminium fix P; at high pH, calcium does. Organic P is released by mineralisation.

sections.heading: Sulphur chemistry
sections.text: Sulphur cycles through organic matter, sulphate and minerals. Microbes mineralise organic S to sulphate (SO4²−), the form plants absorb. Sulphate is an anion, so negative clay surfaces repel it and it leaches easily. At low pH, sulphate is adsorbed on iron and aluminium oxides. Immobilisation occurs when microbes lock sulphate into organic forms. Sulphur deficiency resembles nitrogen deficiency, but yellowing appears first on younger leaves.

sections.heading: Micronutrients and pH
sections.text: Micronutrients are needed in small amounts. Iron, manganese, zinc and copper are cations; boron is mainly boric acid; molybdenum is an anion. Cation availability rises as pH falls, so acid soils can give iron and manganese toxicity. Liming reduces their solubility and can cause zinc or manganese deficiency. Molybdenum behaves oppositely: it is more available at higher pH. Boron has a narrow range; it can leach in acid soils and be adsorbed at high pH. Chelation, binding by organic molecules, keeps iron and zinc in solution. Deficiency symptoms include interveinal chlorosis on young leaves for iron, zinc and manganese; brittle growing points for boron; copper deficiency causes young leaf distortion; and whiptail for molybdenum. Toxicity shows as leaf margin burn for boron and brown spots for manganese.

sections.heading: Field case
sections.text: Suppose a maize field in Kaduna tests pH 5.2. Aluminium and manganese solubility is high, phosphorus is fixed and molybdenum is scarce. Liming towards pH 6.0 can improve P and Mo availability and reduce Al toxicity, but overliming may induce zinc or boron deficiency.

keyPoints: Phosphorus is fixed by iron and aluminium at low pH and by calcium at high pH.
Sulphate is mobile and leachable because it is an anion, but it adsorbs on oxides at low pH.
Cation micronutrients become more soluble at low pH; molybdenum becomes more available at high pH.
Boron has a narrow sufficiency range, so deficiency and toxicity are both possible.
Deficiency symptoms often appear on young leaves for immobile nutrients such as iron, zinc and boron.
Soil pH, organic matter, redox and texture control micronutrient availability, so soil tests guide management.

en.title: Soil Fertility and Plant Nutrition
en.short: Essential nutrients, deficiency diagnosis, soil and leaf testing, and fertiliser rates and timing.

sections.heading: Essential nutrients
sections.text: Higher plants need 17 essential elements. Carbon, hydrogen and oxygen come mainly from air and water. Soil supplies macronutrients (nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, calcium, magnesium, sulphur) in larger amounts and micronutrients (iron, manganese, zinc, copper, boron, molybdenum, chlorine, nickel) in tiny amounts. Nitrogen builds proteins and chlorophyll, phosphorus drives energy transfer, potassium regulates water and enzymes. A shortage of any one limits growth: the law of the minimum.

sections.heading: Deficiency symptoms
sections.text: Deficiency symptoms help diagnosis but do not prove it. Mobile nutrients move from old leaves to new, so nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium and magnesium show first on older leaves: nitrogen gives pale older leaves and stunting, potassium yellow or brown margins, magnesium yellowing between veins. Immobile nutrients such as iron, calcium and boron show on young growth: iron yellowing between veins, calcium distorted new leaves, boron brittle growing points. Other stresses mimic these, so confirm with tests.

sections.heading: Soil and leaf testing
sections.text: Soil testing begins with a representative sample of several cores from the root zone. The laboratory measures pH, organic matter and extractable nutrients. A critical level is the test value below which a response to added nutrient is likely. Levels are calibrated for particular soils, crops and methods, so one region’s method may not suit another. Leaf analysis samples a defined leaf at a defined growth stage, because concentrations change with age, and shows plant uptake. Soil testing guides prevention; leaf analysis checks sufficiency.

sections.heading: Rates and timing
sections.text: A nutrient rate is the mass of nutrient per area, such as kg N per hectare, not the mass of product. Convert: product rate = nutrient rate ÷ fraction of nutrient in the product. To apply 60 kg N/ha with urea (46% N): 60 ÷ 0.46 = 130.4 kg urea/ha. Check: 130.4 × 0.46 = 60.0. Split applications match supply to demand and cut losses; timing and placement depend on nutrient, soil and rainfall. Organic amendments such as manure release nutrients slowly, add organic matter, and vary in content, so analyse them.

keyPoints: Seventeen elements are essential, and a shortage of any one limits growth (law of the minimum).
Mobile nutrients show deficiency on older leaves; immobile ones on young growth.
Symptoms are clues only; confirm with soil tests or leaf analysis.
Soil results are read against critical levels calibrated for local soils, crops and methods.
Product rate = nutrient rate ÷ fraction of nutrient in the product.
Split applications and correct placement match supply to demand and reduce losses.

en.title: Fertilisers, Manures and Nutrient Management Planning
en.short: Straight and compound fertilisers, manures, biofertilisers, label reading, nutrient plans and loss control.

sections.heading: Fertiliser types
sections.text: Straight fertilisers supply one primary nutrient, such as urea for nitrogen. Compound fertilisers supply two or more, chemically made or blended. They save handling but their ratio is fixed, so they may over-supply one nutrient. Organic manures, such as dung, compost and green manure, are low in nutrients but add organic matter and release nutrients slowly. Their composition varies, so test them. Biofertilisers contain live organisms, such as rhizobia for legumes or mycorrhizal fungi. They aid nutrient uptake but do not replace correcting a major deficiency.

sections.heading: Reading a label
sections.text: A label gives nutrient content as percentages by mass, usually nitrogen, phosphate and potash in that order. For example, 20-10-10 means 20% N, 10% P2O5 and 10% K2O. P2O5 and K2O are oxide forms. Multiply P2O5 by about 0.44 to get P, and K2O by about 0.83 to get K. A 50 kg bag of 20-10-10 contains 10 kg N, 5 kg P2O5 and 5 kg K2O. Check the net mass and other nutrients.

sections.heading: Nutrient plan
sections.text: Begin with a soil test and crop nutrient demand. The soil test estimates what the soil itself will supply. Subtract that, and nutrients supplied by manure, legumes or irrigation water. The difference is the fertiliser requirement. Suppose the requirement is 60 kg N, 30 kg P2O5 and 30 kg K2O per hectare. Apply 200 kg/ha of 15-15-15, giving 30 kg N, 30 kg P2O5 and 30 kg K2O. The remaining 30 kg N comes from 65 kg/ha of urea at 46% N, since 30 ÷ 0.46 = 65.2. Split nitrogen and place it near roots. Record and monitor.

sections.heading: Losses and care
sections.text: Nutrients can be lost to water and air. Nitrate leaches into groundwater and rivers. Ammonia volatilises from surface-applied urea and manure, and nitrous oxide forms by denitrification. Runoff carries phosphate and soil into streams. Apply only the calculated amount, split nitrogen, incorporate manure, avoid spreading before heavy rain or on steep wet land, and keep buffer strips beside water. Rules differ by country, so check current national guidance.

keyPoints: Straight fertilisers supply one nutrient; compound fertilisers supply two or more in a fixed ratio.
Organic manures add organic matter and release nutrients slowly; biofertilisers are live organisms that aid uptake.
On a label, N-P-K percentages are by mass; P2O5 × 0.44 gives P and K2O × 0.83 gives K.
Fertiliser requirement = crop nutrient demand − nutrients supplied by the soil (estimated by a soil test), manure, legumes and water.
Worked check: 200 kg/ha of 15-15-15 gives 30 kg each of N, P2O5 and K2O; 65 kg/ha urea at 46% N gives about 30 kg N.
Reduce losses by applying the calculated rate, splitting nitrogen, incorporating manure and keeping buffer strips beside water.

en.title: Soil Conservation and Erosion Control
en.short: Recognising water, wind and tillage erosion and planning contour, terrace, mulch and cover measures.

sections.heading: Erosion types
sections.text: Erosion is the detachment and transport of soil by water, wind or tillage. Sheet erosion removes a thin, fairly uniform layer as raindrops break aggregates and overland flow carries soil away. Rill erosion cuts small channels that normal tillage can smooth. Gully erosion forms deep channels too large to cross with ordinary implements. Wind erosion lifts dry, bare, fine particles and deposits them elsewhere. Tillage erosion is the downslope movement of soil by ploughing and cultivation; soil collects at field edges or bottoms. Sheet and rill erosion often precede gullies.

sections.heading: Risk factors
sections.text: Risk rises with steep or long slopes, intense rain, dry windy weather, fine sandy or weakly structured soil, low organic matter, compaction, bare ground and cultivation up and down the slope. Overgrazing, burning and clearing vegetation remove cover. Cover is usually the factor farmers can change fastest.

sections.heading: Conservation measures
sections.text: Contour farming runs crop rows and tillage across the slope, not up and down, so water slows. Terracing builds level or graded steps to shorten slope length and carry water safely; it needs design and maintenance. Mulching covers the surface with crop residues. Cover crops protect soil in the off-season. Strip cropping alternates close-growing strips with clean-cultivated crops. Agroforestry mixes trees or shrubs with crops; roots and litter improve structure and slow runoff.

sections.heading: Planning on a slope
sections.text: First measure the slope: gradient (%) = rise ÷ run × 100. A field rising 6 m over 50 m has 6 ÷ 50 × 100 = 12%. On gentle slopes, start with contour farming, mulch and cover crops. On steeper land, add terraces or strips, and keep waterways grassed. For example, Musa’s 12% plot in Kaduna should be contoured, not ploughed up and down; maize strips can alternate with cowpea, with mulch and a grassed waterway. Check terraces after storms.

keyPoints: Sheet erosion removes a thin layer; rills are small channels; gullies are too large for normal tillage.
Wind erosion needs dry, bare, fine soil and strong wind; tillage erosion moves soil downslope by cultivation.
Erosion risk rises with steep long slopes, intense rain, weak structure, low cover and up-down cultivation.
Contour farming, terracing, mulching, cover crops, strip cropping and agroforestry slow water and protect cover.
Slope gradient (%) = rise ÷ run × 100; use it to choose measures.
Plan by measuring slope, keeping cover, shortening slope length and checking works after storms.

en.title: Land Evaluation, Capability and Suitability
en.short: Matching land to crops, pasture, forestry or settlement using FAO suitability classes and USDA capability classes.

sections.heading: Matching land to use
sections.text: Land evaluation matches a parcel of land to a use and management system. It compares land qualities, the attributes that affect use, with the requirements of a land use type. Measurable characteristics such as slope, soil depth, drainage and climate are used to judge those qualities. The result shows which uses are physically possible, which need conservation works, and what risks remain. Suitability is specific to a use; capability groups land by broad limitation and risk.

sections.heading: FAO suitability framework
sections.text: FAO’s 1976 Framework for Land Evaluation uses orders: suitable S or not suitable N. Suitable classes are S1 highly suitable, S2 moderately suitable and S3 marginally suitable. Not suitable classes are N1 currently not suitable and N2 permanently not suitable. Subclasses name the main limitation, such as slope or wetness, and units separate management types. The method is iterative: define objectives and land use types, select land qualities, collect data, match, then classify and present. National systems vary, so check local manuals.

sections.heading: Capability classes
sections.text: The USDA land capability classification, widely taught, has eight classes. Classes I to IV are suited to cultivation, with increasing limitations and conservation needs. Classes V to VII are better kept under pasture, forestry or range, and class VIII has no agricultural use. Subclasses use letters for erosion, wetness, soil and climate limits. Capability is broader than suitability: it does not name a crop, but warns how easily land can be damaged.

sections.heading: Limits and a case
sections.text: Slope raises erosion risk and limits machinery; shallow soil restricts roots and water storage; poor drainage causes waterlogging; climate sets the growing season. For settlement, slope, flood risk, drainage and bearing capacity matter, and planning law applies. Example: a 2 ha plot with 15 percent slope, 40 cm soil depth and imperfect drainage is marginal for maize, better for pasture or forestry, and poor for settlement without earthworks. These ratings are illustrative; field survey and local criteria decide.

keyPoints: Land evaluation compares land qualities with the requirements of a defined land use type.
FAO suitability orders are S and N; classes are S1, S2, S3, N1 and N2.
Subclasses name the main limitation, such as slope, wetness, soil depth or climate.
USDA capability classes I to IV are arable; V to VII are pasture, forestry or range; VIII has no agricultural use.
Slope, depth, drainage and climate are common limiting factors for crops, pasture, forestry and settlement.
Settlement suitability needs extra qualities such as flood risk, bearing capacity and planning law.

en.title: Soil Survey, Mapping and Remote Sensing
en.short: Soil survey steps, map scale, mapping units and aerial and satellite support for soil maps.

sections.heading: Survey steps
sections.text: A soil survey starts with a clear objective, because a map for drainage design needs more detail than one for regional planning. Do a desk study of geology, climate, existing maps and land use, then a reconnaissance to choose representative transects and sampling sites. At each site, dig or auger to the required depth, describe the profile horizon by horizon (depth, colour, texture, structure, stones, roots, pH if tested), and take samples from each horizon. Laboratory analysis measures texture, pH, organic carbon, exchangeable cations and other properties named in the objective. Finally, classify the soils, draw boundaries, and produce the map and report.

sections.heading: Scale and mapping units
sections.text: Map scale is the ratio of map distance to ground distance. At 1:25,000, 1 cm on the map represents 25,000 cm, or 250 m, on the ground. A 4 cm by 4 cm square therefore covers 1 km by 1 km, which is 100 hectares. A soil mapping unit is an area drawn on the map with similar soils and landscape; it may contain small inclusions of other soils. The mapping unit is not the same as a taxonomic class such as a soil series.

sections.heading: Remote sensing
sections.text: Aerial photographs show tone, texture, pattern, vegetation and drainage, and overlapping pairs give a stereo view of relief. Satellite images add multispectral bands, which help distinguish bare soil, vegetation and moisture, and digital elevation models help map slope and boundaries. These tools guide where to place observations and how to draw lines between them, but field checking, called ground truthing, is essential. In a small case, a surveyor uses a 1:25,000 aerial photograph to plan a 100 ha block, checks 20 auger points and three pits, then adjusts the map boundaries after laboratory results.

keyPoints: A soil survey begins with an objective and a desk study, then uses reconnaissance, profile description, sampling, laboratory analysis and map production.
Map scale is map distance divided by ground distance; at 1:25,000, 1 cm represents 250 m.
Ground area = map area × (scale denominator)², with both areas in the same units.
A soil mapping unit is a mapped area with similar soils and landscape, and it may contain inclusions.
Aerial photographs and satellite images guide boundary drawing and sampling but need field ground truthing.
Laboratory data and field observations must be checked before the final map and report are issued.

en.title: Measuring Soil Moisture and the Field Water Balance
en.short: Methods for measuring soil water, and using a field water balance to schedule irrigation.

sections.heading: Measuring water content
sections.text: Gravimetric sampling is the reference method: weigh moist soil, oven dry it at 105 °C to constant mass, and calculate mass water ÷ dry soil mass. Multiply by dry bulk density to get volumetric water content, θv, the volume of water per volume of soil. It is accurate but destructive and slow. A tensiometer measures matric potential, the suction plants must overcome. It is cheap in wet soil, but needs a water retention curve to give water content and fails when very dry. A neutron probe measures θv by counting thermalised neutrons around an access tube; it is good for deep profiles but needs site calibration and radiation precautions. Time domain reflectometry (TDR) estimates θv from the soil’s dielectric permittivity; it is fast and repeatable, but salinity and clay may need calibration.

sections.heading: Field water balance
sections.text: For a root zone of depth Z, storage S = θv × Z. Over a period, ΔS = P + I − ET − D − R, where P is rainfall, I irrigation, ET evapotranspiration, D drainage below the root zone and R runoff, all in mm. Measure P and I directly, estimate ET from weather data, and measure S or θv. The balance shows whether the root zone gains or loses water.

sections.heading: Scheduling example
sections.text: Take Z = 600 mm, field capacity θv = 0.30, and current θv = 0.20. Storage at field capacity = 0.30 × 600 = 180 mm; current storage = 0.20 × 600 = 120 mm; deficit = 60 mm. In one day, P = 10 mm, ET = 5 mm, and D = R = 0. Then ΔS = 10 − 5 = 5 mm, so new storage = 125 mm and the deficit is 55 mm. To refill to field capacity, apply 55 mm of net irrigation. If irrigation efficiency is 0.75, gross irrigation = 55 ÷ 0.75 = 73.3 mm. Schedule before storage falls below the allowable depletion limit, not after stress appears.

keyPoints: Gravimetric water content = mass water ÷ dry soil mass; volumetric water content = gravimetric water content × dry bulk density.
Tensiometers measure matric potential, not water content directly, and need a retention curve for conversion.
Neutron probes and time domain reflectometry measure volumetric water content, but both need calibration for local soil conditions.
Field water balance: ΔS = P + I − ET − D − R, with all terms in mm for the root zone.
Gross irrigation requirement = (field capacity storage − current storage) ÷ irrigation efficiency.
Schedule irrigation before the allowable depletion limit is reached, not after the crop shows stress.

en.title: Irrigation and Drainage Principles
en.short: How soil texture, structure and depth set irrigation interval, and how surface, sprinkler, drip and drainage work.

sections.heading: Storage and interval
sections.text:
Available water capacity (AWC) is water held between field capacity and permanent wilting point. Texture sets the amount: sands hold little, clays hold more but may release it slowly, and loams often balance the two. Structure controls pores; compaction restricts roots and reduces the soil volume explored. Depth sets the root zone. Shallow soil or a hardpan stores less water, so crops need lighter, more frequent irrigation.

The irrigation interval is the time before allowable depletion is reached:
interval = (AWC × root depth × allowable depletion) ÷ crop water use.
Example: AWC = 0.18 m³/m³, root depth = 0.6 m, allowable depletion = 0.5, crop use = 5 mm/day.
Total available = 0.18 × 0.6 = 0.108 m = 108 mm.
Allowable = 108 × 0.5 = 54 mm.
Interval = 54 ÷ 5 = 10.8 days, about 11 days.
Allowable depletion is the fraction of AWC usable before stress. Check local evapotranspiration and rainfall; the interval changes as the crop grows.

sections.heading: Irrigation methods
sections.text:
Surface irrigation lets water flow over the soil by gravity in basins, borders or furrows. It is cheap but needs level land and careful stream size; uneven infiltration causes over- and under-watering.

Sprinkler irrigation sprays pressurised water through nozzles, like rain. It suits uneven land and can apply small amounts, but wind and evaporation reduce uniformity.

Drip irrigation delivers water through emitters to the root zone, often frequently. It uses little water and limits weed growth, but filters, flushing and clogging need management. Salts can accumulate at the wetting front, so occasional leaching may be needed.

sections.heading: Drainage principles
sections.text: Waterlogging fills soil pores with water and lowers oxygen. Surface drainage removes runoff and ponded water using graded land, ditches or channels. Subsurface drainage uses buried pipes or mole drains to lower the water table. In saline land, drainage is combined with leaching: extra water pushes salts below the root zone, and the salty outflow must be safely disposed of.

keyPoints: Available water capacity depends on texture, structure and root-zone depth.
Irrigation interval = (AWC × root depth × allowable depletion) ÷ crop water use, with consistent units.
Surface irrigation is cheap but needs level land and even infiltration.
Sprinkler systems can suit uneven land but wind and evaporation reduce efficiency.
Drip irrigation is efficient but needs filtration and flushing to prevent clogging.
Drainage lowers water tables; saline land needs drainage plus leaching and safe disposal of salty outflow.

en.title: Saline, Sodic and Acid Sulphate Soils: Damage and Reclamation
en.short: Chemistry and damage of saline, sodic and acid sulphate soils, and their reclamation.

sections.heading: Three problem soils
sections.text:
Saline soils hold enough soluble salt to raise the electrical conductivity of the saturated paste extract above about 4 dS/m, but little exchangeable sodium (ESP below about 15%), and pH is usually below 8.5. Crops suffer osmotic drought: roots cannot draw water even from moist soil, and chloride or sodium may be toxic. Structure stays sound.

Sodic soils carry high exchangeable sodium (ESP above about 15%, or a sodium adsorption ratio above about 13). Sodium disperses clay, so aggregates slake, pores seal, infiltration slows and a hard crust forms. pH often exceeds 8.5.

Acid sulphate soils contain pyrite. Drainage admits air, the pyrite oxidises to sulfuric acid, pH falls below 4 and toxic aluminium is released. These thresholds vary between classification systems, so check which one you use.

sections.heading: Reclamation methods
sections.text:
Saline soils are reclaimed by leaching: water applied beyond crop need pushes salts downward, and subsurface drains carry them away. Without drainage the water table rises and the salt returns.

Sodic soils need calcium first. Gypsum dissolves, its calcium displaces sodium from the exchange sites, and drainage removes the sodium. Lime suits acid soils, not sodic ones, because calcium carbonate barely dissolves at high pH. Acid sulphate soils are safest kept waterlogged; where they must be drained, lime the topsoil and avoid deep drains.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text:
Gypsum requirement. Soil: CEC 20 cmolc/kg, ESP 30%, target ESP 10%, bulk density 1.3 g/cm³, depth 0.15 m.
Sodium to replace = (30 − 10) ÷ 100 × 20 = 4 cmolc/kg.
Gypsum per cmolc of calcium = 0.861 g, since CaSO4·2H2O is about 23% calcium.
Gypsum = 4 × 0.861 = 3.44 g/kg.
Soil mass per hectare = 10,000 × 0.15 × 1,300 = 1,950,000 kg.
Gypsum = 3.44 × 1,950,000 = 6,700,000 g, about 6.7 t/ha.
Field rates are raised for purity and uneven mixing.

sections.heading: Secondary salinisation
sections.text: Irrigation without drainage raises the water table. Salts in the irrigation water remain when water evaporates, and capillary rise brings more to the surface, leaving white crusts and killing seedlings. Prevention and cure are the same: irrigate to crop need, keep the water table below the root zone, and maintain drains. Water quality and local rules vary, so check current local guidance.

keyPoints: Saline soils have high soluble salts and low ESP; sodic soils have high ESP and disperse.
Salinity causes osmotic drought; sodicity destroys structure and infiltration.
Acid sulphate soils acidify when drained, releasing aluminium.
Leaching removes salts only if drainage carries them away.
Gypsum supplies calcium for sodic soils; lime corrects acidity, not sodicity.
Irrigation without drainage causes secondary salinisation.

en.title: Soil Pollution, Waste Disposal and Remediation
en.short: Contaminant sources, how pollutants move through soil, and prevention, monitoring and clean-up.

sections.heading: Where contaminants come from
sections.text:
Industry releases heavy metals such as lead, cadmium and mercury, solvents and petroleum hydrocarbons. Mining leaves tailings and spoil heaps rich in arsenic, lead and sulphides; oxidising sulphides form sulphuric acid, and acid mine drainage releases metals into streams. Sewage carries pathogens, nitrate, phosphate and metals. Agrochemicals add pesticides, nitrate from excess fertiliser and copper fungicides.

A pollutant is a substance present where it does harm. Harm depends on concentration, chemical form and pathway, not total amount alone.

sections.heading: How they move
sections.text:
Soluble pollutants such as nitrate and many pesticides leach with drainage water. Metals bind strongly to clay and organic matter, so they mostly stay near the surface, but a fall in pH releases them into solution. Water moves faster down cracks and worm channels than through the soil matrix; this preferential flow can carry contaminants quickly to groundwater.

Erosion and runoff wash contaminated topsoil into streams.

sections.heading: Prevention and monitoring
sections.text:
Prevention is cheaper than cure. Use less hazardous materials, line waste pits and landfills with clay or synthetic liners, separate clean from dirty water, and keep vegetated buffer strips beside streams.

Monitoring means repeated soil sampling and groundwater wells, compared with a reference site or a legal limit. Limit values differ by country and land use, so check the current national standard or WHO drinking-water guidelines.

sections.heading: Remediation and its limits
sections.text:
Containment, such as a cap or barrier wall, isolates waste but does not destroy it and needs long-term care. Bioremediation uses micro-organisms to break down organic pollutants; it suits petroleum hydrocarbons but cannot remove metals, which cannot be destroyed. Phytoremediation uses plants: phytoextraction draws metals into harvestable shoots, while rhizodegradation supports microbes in the root zone. It is cheap for large, lightly polluted areas but slow, limited by root depth, and the harvested biomass is hazardous waste.

Case: Amina’s market garden near a Nigerian town was irrigated with raw sewage for years; soil tests show high lead. The source is cut off, food crops stop, and phytoextraction with monitoring begins.

keyPoints: Contaminants reach soil from industry, mining, sewage and agrochemicals, and harm depends on concentration, chemical form and pathway.
Soluble pollutants such as nitrate leach, while metals stay sorbed to clay and organic matter until pH falls.
Preferential flow down cracks and channels can carry contaminants quickly to groundwater.
Prevention by source control, liners and buffer strips is cheaper and more reliable than clean-up.
Bioremediation destroys organic pollutants but cannot remove metals, which are elements.
Phytoremediation is cheap but slow, limited by root depth, and leaves contaminated biomass that must be disposed of safely.

en.title: Soils of Nigeria and Africa: Distribution and Management
en.short: Major African soil groups, where they occur, their management problems and farmers’ responses.

sections.heading: Groups and distribution
sections.text: The names used here are World Reference Base (WRB) groups, an international classification. Ferralsols are deep, strongly weathered red or yellow soils, rich in iron and aluminium oxides and low in weatherable minerals. They dominate the humid Congo Basin and parts of the forest and derived savanna zones of West Africa, including southern Nigeria. Acrisols are also strongly weathered but acidic, with low base saturation and a clay-enriched subsoil. They occur in humid and subhumid West Africa and southern Nigeria. Lixisols are weathered soils with high base saturation, common in the drier savannas. Vertisols are clay-rich shrink-swell soils of flat plains and alluvial flats. Fluvisols, commonly called alluvial soils, are young, layered soils of floodplains, deltas and valleys, such as Nigeria’s Niger Delta and fadama lands (seasonally flooded lowlands).

sections.heading: Ferralsols and Acrisols
sections.text: Both groups have low cation exchange capacity and few nutrient reserves. Acrisols are often strongly acid, so aluminium can be toxic and phosphorus is fixed. Ferralsols can be productive but need inputs. Farmers use fallow, agroforestry, cover crops, mulching, manure and lime where acidity limits crops. On slopes, erosion is a risk.

sections.heading: Savanna and floodplain soils
sections.text: Lixisols suffer surface crusting, low organic matter and nutrient depletion; farmers use manure, rotations with legumes, tied ridges and water harvesting. Vertisols crack when dry and become sticky when wet, giving a narrow tillage window and waterlogging; broad-bed and furrow systems, ridges and drainage help. Alluvial soils vary in texture and fertility and flood often; farmers use flood-recession cropping, fadama irrigation and raised beds.

sections.heading: A small case
sections.text: Suppose Amina farms a lixisol in Nigeria’s Guinea savanna. Her field crusts after rain, and maize yields fall without manure. She spreads cattle manure, rotates maize with cowpea and uses tied ridges to hold water. These practices treat the soil’s weaknesses rather than only adding fertiliser.

keyPoints: Ferralsols and Acrisols are strongly weathered, low-CEC soils of humid Africa; Acrisols are also acid and low in base saturation.
Lixisols are weathered savanna soils with high base saturation; they crust and lose organic matter easily.
Vertisols are shrink-swell clays with a narrow tillage window and waterlogging risk.
Alluvial soils (Fluvisols) are young floodplain soils, variable in texture and fertility and prone to flooding.
Farmers respond with fallow, agroforestry, manure, lime, tied ridges, broad-bed and furrow, and flood-recession or fadama farming.
Soil group names follow the WRB; local maps and fertility vary, so check local survey data.

en.title: Land Use Change, Soil Carbon and Climate
en.short: How deforestation, cultivation and grazing change soil carbon and greenhouse gases, and how stocks are measured.

sections.heading: Land use effects
sections.text: Soil organic carbon (SOC) is carbon in soil organic matter. Deforestation removes litter and roots, warms soil and speeds decomposition, so SOC falls and CO2 is released; erosion adds loss. Cultivation breaks aggregates, exposes protected organic matter to microbes and lowers residue inputs, causing rapid SOC loss before a new lower level. Grazing varies with intensity: light or moderate grazing can maintain SOC through dung and litter, while heavy grazing reduces cover, compacts soil and causes erosion and SOC loss.

sections.heading: Greenhouse gas fluxes
sections.text: Greenhouse gases (GHGs) trap heat. Carbon dioxide comes from decomposing organic matter; nitrous oxide (N2O) mainly from nitrogen fertiliser, manure and dung, especially in wet or compacted soil; methane (CH4) from anaerobic soils such as flooded paddies and from ruminant digestion. Land use change can turn a soil sink into a source. Well-aerated, covered soil with steady organic inputs tends to store carbon and emit less N2O, but climate, texture and management matter.

sections.heading: Measuring carbon stocks
sections.text:
SOC stock is carbon mass per area in a stated layer, in t C/ha. A field estimate uses:
SOC stock (t C/ha) = SOC (g/kg) × bulk density (g/cm³) × depth (cm) × 0.1.
For example, 10 g/kg, 1.3 g/cm³ and 30 cm give 10 × 1.3 × 30 × 0.1 = 39 t C/ha. Bulk density is dry soil mass per volume. Because land use changes bulk density, compare stocks on an equivalent soil mass basis: the carbon in the same mass of soil, not the same depth. Use replicated sampling and laboratory analysis, with models or remote sensing for mapping; uncertainty is often large.

sections.heading: Projects and climate-smart farming
sections.text: Soil carbon projects pay for practices that add or protect SOC, such as agroforestry, cover crops, reduced tillage and improved grazing. They must show additionality (extra carbon beyond baseline), permanence (lasting storage), no leakage (emissions elsewhere) and monitoring, reporting and verification (MRV). Climate-smart agriculture aims to raise productivity, build resilience and cut emissions where possible; it does not guarantee large gains. Rules vary by country and standard, so check official guidance.

keyPoints: Deforestation and cultivation usually lower SOC by cutting inputs and speeding decomposition; heavy grazing does too, while moderate grazing may maintain it.
SOC stock (t C/ha) = SOC (g/kg) × bulk density (g/cm³) × depth (cm) × 0.1.
Compare land uses on an equivalent soil mass basis because bulk density changes with management.
N2O comes mainly from nitrogen inputs in wet or compacted soil; CH4 from anaerobic soils and ruminants; CO2 from decomposition.
Soil carbon projects need additionality, permanence, no leakage and monitoring, reporting and verification.
Climate-smart agriculture pursues productivity, resilience and lower emissions, but soil carbon gains are finite and reversible.

en.title: Soil Biology in Sustainable Agriculture
en.short: How five farming practices feed soil life, and how conservation and conventional agriculture compare.

sections.heading: Practices that feed soil
sections.text:
Crop rotation means growing different crops in sequence on the same land. Different roots release different sugars and acids, feeding different microbes, and rotation breaks pest cycles. Residue management means leaving crop leftovers on the field instead of burning or removing them. Residues shield the surface, feed earthworms and fungi, and add carbon. Reduced tillage means less ploughing, or none (no-till). Less disturbance keeps fungal networks and earthworm burrows intact.

Cover crops are plants grown between main crops to cover bare soil. Their roots feed microbes and their canopy protects aggregates from rain. Agroforestry means growing trees with crops. Tree roots and litter support mycorrhizal fungi (root-partnering fungi), and shade reduces heat stress on soil life. Together these practices build soil structure: the arrangement of particles into aggregates, the crumbs that hold pores open.

sections.heading: Conservation versus conventional
sections.text:
Conservation agriculture (CA) rests on three principles: minimum soil disturbance, permanent soil cover, and crop diversification. Conventional agriculture here means ploughing, residue removal or burning, and often monoculture. On soil health indicators such as organic carbon, aggregate stability, infiltration and earthworm numbers, long-term CA usually scores higher. The gain is slow and depends on climate and residue supply.

Yield risk differs. CA can reduce yield in the first years, especially where residues are scarce or soils are cold and wet, and it may need more herbicides. In dry years, CA often yields more because cover and structure hold water. Conventional tillage gives quick seedbed preparation and can bury weeds, but it depletes organic matter and leaves soil bare.

sections.heading: A small case
sections.text:
